item.title: What's Wrong With Alexithymia?
item.description:
Alexithymia

What's Wrong With Alexithymia?

Some people have difficulty verbalizing emotions. But that is not a "disorder."

Posted June 17, 2026

Source: Liza Summer/Pexels

I have worked with many clients who identify, or have been identified, as "alexithymic." I find this a somewhat forbidding diagnostic term, so I like to take some time to share what exactly alexithymia is and why, and when, it is something to be addressed in therapy.

To begin, the formal definition: "alexithymia" is literally a failure of being unable ("a-" for lack) to understand certain words (that's the "lexi") for emotions ("-thymia" being a general psychological suffix being used in this context to denote emotion or affect). Put in these terms, alexithymia is a certain kind of aspect of verbal processing. When the term was introduced in the 1970s, it was meant to recall "dyslexia," another term used to describe a certain kind of atypical relationship to words and language.

The first thing to note is that alexithymia is not a psychiatric disorder of the kind enumerated in a diagnostic manual like the the DSM. Your psychiatrist or therapist cannot diagnose you as alexithymic, as she can diagnose you with Major Depressive Disorder or Generalized Anxiety Disorder. Alexithymia is, at most, a symptom, or perhaps a certain way of framing a certain constellation of symptoms—although it is not even included as a symptom in many diagnostic manuals. It is correlated with certain recognized disorders, notably Autism Spectrum Disorder, but it is not itself a diagnosis.

I emphasize these points because there is a widespread tendency to reify alexithymia and make it perhaps something more than it is. Searching online finds it described as "emotion blindness," a "neuropsychological phenomenon," or a "personality trait." A person with alexithymia may display one or more of these tendencies, but in itself alexithymia is a behavioral or even conversational tendency and is not to be identified with any of these.

Is alexithymia a problem, something that demands treatment or remediation? My view is that it depends. Sometimes this kind of limitation in affective processing can be an obstacle to someone's goals and projects. Often this may include her personal relationships, but it may include her work as well, especially if her work requires a high degree of emotional awareness.

But other times this is not so. A person can manage perfectly well with an alexithymic disposition, and may even endorse it as a part of her personality. In the same way a person who is visually blind may see her condition as part of who she is, not something to be cured, so may someone who is "emotionally blind" (to use for a moment that fraught metaphor) be perfectly happy with herself and her relationship to the emotional world.

Many therapists endorse this kind of pluralistic and tolerant view for a range of psychological dispositions. It is generally recognized, at least in many corners of mental health care, that we should not understand the mind in terms of deficits that are to be somehow remedied, but in terms of helping someone to flourish whatever her particular mental dispositions may be.

Yet this attitude is not always carried over to the case of alexithymia. There are at least two reasons, I think, why this is not so.

One is a sort of professional bias. If you ask a professional basketball player how to improve your life, she may well say: Play more basketball. That is how she makes her living, and likely how she prefers to spend her free time too, so she will be very inclined to recommend it to others. In the same way, if you ask a therapist how to improve your life, she will likely say: Talk more about your emotions. This is partly because this is indeed a good thing to do (as is playing basketball), but that is likely not all that lies behind her recommendation. She, like the basketball player, tends to be influenced by the norms and habits of her profession, and one norm of her profession is to talk about one's emotions. Indeed, in certain views, psychotherapy ultimately is nothing but the making explicit of one's emotional life. So it is natural that a therapist will tend to recommend this, and will also tend to be concerned when this kind of verbalizing capacity appears to be different or atypical.

Here I think the therapist must take great care. Is a given person's alexithymia hindering her ability to live the kind of life that she wants to live? Or is it simply limiting her ability to participate in some of the standard conventions of therapy? It will depend on the client, and it is not clear, in the abstract, which of these interpretations is the correct one.

The second reason has to do with our ever-progressing understanding of neurodiversity. I noted above that there is a strong correlation between alexithymia and Autism Spectrum Disorder. There is an increasing recognition that Autism Spectrum Disorder is not really a disorder at all, but rather a distinctive kind of psychology with its own particular characteristics. This is an easy view to embrace when we consider the "strengths" associated with Autism Spectrum Disorder, but less obvious when we consider "weaknesses" such as alexithymia. But, if we take seriously the point of view of neurodiversity, the language of strength and weakness is inapt. The diversity in neurodiversity is simply evaluatively neutral, and in some deep sense a tendency such as alexithymia, considered in itself, is neither good nor bad.

None of this is to say that alexithymia cannot, or should not, be addressed. I often do so myself in my own work. But it is to emphasize that there are a number of pressures to do so that are, on consideration, illegitimate. These include a model of neurodiversity that is framed in terms of deficits, and therapists' own understandable bias toward emotional talk. The proper reasons for addressing alexithymia, when they are present, should come not from the therapist's expectations of what is typical but rather from the client herself.

item.title: The People Who Witness Us
item.description:
Grief

The People Who Witness Us

Personal Perspective: Remembering Robert Thurman, and the few who see us clearly

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • A relationship’s importance isn’t measured by its duration.
  • We often don’t recognize who holds up our lives until they’re gone.
  • Being seen accurately brings relief, because it ends the labor of explaining ourselves.
Bob Thurman in 2014
Source: Christopher Michel / CC BY-SA 4.0

Today I learned that Robert Thurman had died.

The sadness made sense. The surprise didn’t. Not the surprise that he’d died—he was 84, and death at that age arrives more or less on schedule. What caught me off guard was how much space he turned out to occupy inside me. It shouldn’t have hit the way it did.

We only knew each other for a short time. He read my book, offered a testimonial, and came to my launch. A few months ago, I joined him on his podcast to discuss the ideas that had brought us together. By any objective measure, hardly any time at all. Yet when I heard the news, something important seemed to shift.

It made me think about an illusion many of us carry: that the importance of a relationship is determined by its duration. A 20-year friendship should matter more than a two-year one. A spouse more than a teacher. A lifelong colleague more than someone we met only recently.

But our inner lives don’t organize themselves by the calendar. Some people occupy decades and leave barely a trace. Others enter briefly and become part of the architecture.

Psychologists talk about attachment figures—the people who give us safety, guidance, stability. We picture parents, partners, close friends. But as I’ve gotten older, I’ve come to suspect there is another category altogether: the people who witness us.

Not necessarily the people who know us best. The people who see us most clearly. Many people know our history. Few recognize our essence. And when someone does, something unusual happens. We relax.

Self-verification theory holds that human beings seek confirmation of who they believe themselves to be—and that this isn’t vanity but a hunger for coherence. We spend enormous energy managing the gap between how we’re perceived and who we feel we are. When someone sees us accurately, that labor stops. The gap closes. For a moment, we don’t have to convince anyone of anything. That, I think, is why being truly seen feels less like flattery and more like relief.

Bob had a way of doing this that I keep returning to. When he wrote about my book, he didn’t reach for the usual blurb language; he said reading it felt like going on a journey with a friend whose honest reckoning with life and death stirred the same reflections in him about his own. He’d let the book do something to him, and he admitted it.

He did the same on the podcast, where he confessed that he’d first assumed I was an atheist when in fact I’m agnostic—and that he hadn’t had much respect for atheists until he read my book. A strange, backhanded, wonderful thing to say. It landed because it was specific. He hadn’t filed me into a category. He’d read me, gotten me slightly wrong, corrected himself, and let the encounter change something in him.

There was a smaller moment, too. At my launch, mid-speech, I did the thing writers do—I minimized the book, waved it off, got self-deprecating. Bob interrupted me. He wanted it on the record that the book was very good. Period. The man who had just called it extraordinary would not sit there and watch me shrink it.

Most writers spend years sending signals into the world without knowing where they land. We sit alone with ideas and questions, publish them, and hope they reach someone. Usually, we never find out. Occasionally, the signal reaches a person whose own work has already become part of our internal landscape—and when that person answers, it can feel almost surreal. Not because it validates the work. Because it validates you.

Looking back, I notice that some of the most important people in my life arrived exactly this way. People who appeared briefly and altered my trajectory. Erik Erikson named a stage of late development generativity—the desire to nurture those who come after us. The healthiest elders, he suggested, become gardeners; they invest in futures they may never see. Bob embodied that, not only through his scholarship but through his readiness to encourage someone he’d only recently met. He always looked you in the eye with a bright smile, as if the conversation in front of him were the only one that mattered.

I suspect most of us are carrying invisible pieces of people who shaped us. A sentence from a teacher. A book that arrived at the right moment. A person who saw something in us before we saw it ourselves. They become part of the hidden structure holding up our lives, and we rarely think about them.

Until they’re gone. Then suddenly we see the beams, the pillars, the supports that helped us become who we are. Death has a strange way of revealing what life concealed; the architecture becomes visible only when one of its supports is removed.

So today I’m grateful—not only for Robert Thurman’s life, but for what his death makes visible. None of us truly knows the effect we have on others. A conversation we barely remember may become someone’s turning point. A refusal to let someone minimize their own work may outlast the person who refused.

We move through the world believing our influence is measured by our achievements. Maybe it’s measured by something quieter—how clearly we manage to see the people who cross our path, and whether, in being seen, they get to set down for a moment the weight of explaining themselves.

Bob saw me. He looked me in the eye, smiled, and wouldn’t let me shrink.

item.title: Improve Your Well-being With a Walk Audit
item.description:
Positive Psychology

Improve Your Well-being With a Walk Audit

Tending to your environment is key to thriving.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Small changes to your physical surroundings can lead to big payoffs.
  • Well-being and resilience are based on the physical environment too, not just our inner world.
  • Apply the walk audit—a tool from urban planning—to enhance your life.

Most of psychology focuses on our inner experiences or our relationships with other humans. These are important, but they don’t happen in a void. Our physical environments shape our experiences and impact our well-being and resilience too.

One especially neglected area is the built environment. These are the human-made spaces where most of us spend most of our time.

Our physical environments can support our well-being and ability to overcome challenges (resilience)--or not. Everyone knows that generic cubicles and ugly fluorescent lighting can be soul-sucking environments, but there’s more to it than that—and a walk audit can help you maximize your surroundings.

Working on our physical spaces pays off 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Sometimes it is hard to exercise, meditate, or journal. We might be too sick, busy, or dealing with crises. A supportive physical environment can help sustain you through those times. It’s a key element of our resilience portfolios. Also, tweaking the physical environment can help many people at once.

How to Conduct a Walk Audit

A walk audit is a simple tool that involves intentionally moving through the spaces of your life, and trying to see them with fresh eyes.

Choose one space at a time to focus on: workplace, school, home, or somewhere else.

Slow down and try to remember your first impressions of the space. Take at least 10-15 minutes to walk around (longer if it is a big space), and then process what you observed. It can be good to walk with others who use the space.

Consider the following. Feel free to take photos or videos as you walk.

Before You Walk

Take a moment to revisit previous thoughts or comments about the space:

  • Do people often get lost trying to find it?
  • Do visitors seem unsure where to sit or stand?
  • Are you comfortable in this space, or do long hours in this space leave you with a sore back or neck?
  • What positive compliments have you received about the space?
  • What is your favorite element?

During Your Walk Audit

1. Think about how easily a newcomer can navigate your space.

  • Are there signs that help visitors find their way—clearly visible house numbers, buildings, departments, classrooms?
  • Do safe sidewalks or pathways naturally direct people to the reception or other key areas?

2. How welcoming is your space?

  • Are there signs that greet or welcome people?
  • Are there plants, flowers, art, or other landscaping or décor that make the place appealing to approach?

3. Are your family/organizational/institutional values readily apparent from the surroundings? This could manifest itself in various ways:

  • At school or work, perhaps the simplest is just to post your mission statement or institutional values where people can see them.
  • Upkeep is a signal to people about whether your institution is important to the people who inhabit it.
  • Photographs can be a huge help here. In the home, photographs can show a commitment to family or send a message about a love of travel or a favorite hobby. At work or school, people can be highlighted for good performance, or showcased for volunteering for a cause that the organization supports.

4. Do the surroundings promote well-being through warm or vibrant (versus sterile) color choices, comfortable furnishings, and quiet and privacy when needed?

  • Some workplaces need to protect employees’ privacy, but that doesn’t mean that a place has to look soulless. If you can't post family photos, consider a child's drawing or a souvenir.
  • Appealing paint colors, nice lighting, murals, and upholstered furniture all indicate that these are places where people can be happy.

5. Are the surroundings appropriate for the population?

  • If children are often in the space, are there books and toys for them? Child-sized furniture?
  • If groups are often in the space, is the seating arranged so that people from the same family, classroom, or department can sit together?
  • If the community visits the space, are there comfortable places for them?

6. Are there accessibility issues for people with disabilities?

  • Are there ramps and handicap-accessible bathrooms?
  • Is there clutter that makes it hard for people to pass, or signage that is too small for many people to read?

7. Are basic human/mammalian needs being met?

  • Are there bathrooms, kitchens, fridges, opportunities to eat, exercise, rest?
  • Is there a break room or a place where people can catch up informally?

8. Think about the arrangement of furniture in indoor spaces. What messages does that send?

  • In office or school spaces, one thing I always notice is how chairs are arranged around a desk. I like to put a chair on the side of my desk for visitors, which feels less formal and intimidating. Or set things up so you can pivot your chair away from your desk and join a circle of chairs. A huge desk with a big office chair on one side and smaller furniture opposite indicates emotional distance and hierarchies.
  • In home spaces, some living rooms or dens only have one comfortable chair, for the head of the household. Everyone else shifts and fidgets.

What is one change you could make today that would improve your space?

Some examples that don’t cost any money:

  • Create a sign (just use a regular printer) that is more informative or welcoming, or that reinforces institutional values.
  • Move some furniture around to encourage more interaction.
  • Remove an obstacle or unused equipment.
  • Clean up an area. Start small: Clear out a shelf, closet, or drawer. Small steps add up.

Some inexpensive examples:

  • Purchase and install (it just takes a few screws or nails) some larger and nicer house numbers.
  • Get some inexpensive frames (black ones look nice at almost any price point) and frame some pictures from some children, that statement of values you just printed, or a favorite quote.
  • Repaint your space, or buy inexpensive art at a thrift store or yard sale to cover blemishes.
  • Bring less-industrial furniture into your work or school space. Used furniture prices are perhaps as cheap as they’ve ever been, and a lot of that furniture is much nicer quality than you can buy new in most stores.
  • Add some desk or floor lamps so that overhead lighting is not the only kind. Change the lightbulbs to warmer or rosier colors.

Small changes can lead to big, lasting payoffs that require little or no ongoing effort. Don’t neglect this key tool for enhancing your resilience and well-being—as well as helping those you care about.

My new book, Stronger Than You Think: Building Lifelong Resilience (Penguin Random House, 2026), offers additional ideas for enhancing your physical environment and other elements of your resilience portfolio.

item.title: The Illness That Hides Itself
item.description:
Mania

The Illness That Hides Itself

In mania, self-knowledge is the first thing the illness takes.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Anosognosia is not denial. It is a neurological failure of the brain's ability to recognize its own illness.
  • It affects up to 98 percent of people with schizophrenia and 63 percent of those with bipolar I disorder.
  • The manic mind does not experience its own blindness as blindness. It experiences it as truth.
  • Recognizing that self-knowledge itself can break is where the reckoning of recovery begins.
Source: Damir K./Pexels

The pills sat in my palm like a verdict.

One was the color of Pepto-Bismol—Depakote, a mood stabilizer. The other was white—Zyprexa, an antipsychotic. They had been prescribed by a tall, imposing psychiatrist at St. Mary's Hospital following weeks in which I had, among other things: waged a public campaign against a former employer whose conduct I believed, not without basis, warranted exposure; amplified claims about him online that went well beyond what I could substantiate; demanded $5,000 from my mother via PayPal as proof of love; and left her a voicemail, a cry of manic anguish that crossed into threat, in which I screamed that I would end her life if she didn't leave me alone.

This I had experienced as speaking truth to power.

I sat in my home, looked at the pink pill and the white one, and flushed them down the toilet. It felt like an act of sovereignty—the mind, certain of itself, refusing the medicine that would have calmed it.

Last week I wrote about what mania feels like from the inside: the seduction of certainty, the sense of finally arriving. But there is a layer beneath that seduction that took me longer to understand. Not why mania feels like insight, but why a person who has already been told he is ill will still flush the pills. That layer has a clinical name: Anosognosia.

The word is Greek: without knowledge of disease. It describes a failure of self-updating—a breakdown in the brain's ability to revise its picture of itself when the evidence changes. And what makes it so treacherous is not the gap it creates but the fact that the gap is unfelt.

This is what separates it from denial, and the distinction matters more than it might seem. A person in denial, on some level, knows. The knowledge is buried, avoided, kept at a distance—but somewhere inside, a self has registered the truth and is working to keep it at bay. A person with anosognosia does not know. The circuit that would generate the knowledge is offline. The mirror has not been refused. It has been shattered, and the shards reassembled into a reflection that no longer corresponds to anything real.

The philosopher Jonathan Lear writes that "a person is, by his nature, out of touch with his own subjectivity... even if he is sincere, he won't know the answer." Even someone genuinely trying to see himself clearly may be constitutionally unable to do so—and the trying changes nothing.

Most illnesses are transparent to their subjects. You know you have a fever, a broken leg, a headache. The feeling of wrongness is itself information, and it points you toward help. Severe psychiatric illness can take that capacity away. The very instrument you would use to notice that something is wrong is the one that's broken—and the loss is invisible, which is what makes it so dangerous, and so hard for everyone around the person to understand.

Studies estimate that anosognosia affects between 50 and 98 percent of people with schizophrenia and between 35 and 63 percent of those with bipolar I disorder, though estimates vary depending on how the condition is measured and how severe the threshold is set. Nassir Ghaemi, the psychiatrist and philosopher of medicine, describes it as one end of a spectrum: at the mild end, a person underestimates how serious their illness is; at the far end, the illness has colonized the very faculty that would otherwise report it.

The clinical psychologist Xavier Amador has developed an analogy that families tend to find clarifying. Imagine someone told you that you did not live where you live. You would laugh. What if they then produced a court order requiring you to stay away from what you know is your home address? What if the people you lived with had signed off on that order and told you, voices strained, that if you came around again they would call the police? What if you were taken to a hospital and given medication for a "delusion" that you lived where you know you live? Would you take that medication?

Of course not. Because it's the truth.

That is what it is like for a person with severe mental illness to have a delusion and anosognosia simultaneously. The certainty is indistinguishable from sanity. More than indistinguishable: it feels, from the inside, like the only sanity available.

What I could have told you during those years—the years of cycling depression and manic resurgence, further hospitalizations, substance use through the depressive troughs—is that bipolar disorder was a real condition affecting real people. I was an academic who had encountered the clinical literature at the edges of his training and could discuss it fluently. I knew the illness the way a drowning man might know the physics of water.

What I could not do was apply any of it to myself. The knowledge sat in a separate room from the life I was living, and the door between them was sealed.

What gets lost in this condition isn't only information. It's the soul—the small interior voice that says wait, that slows a person down before a decision, that makes room for another person's version of events. The mind, in mania, runs unchecked. The soul, which would otherwise question and temper it, goes quiet. And the story the mind tells about itself continues, unchallenged, no matter what it costs.

My mother, Linda, a nurse and bioethicist, watched me deteriorate across a decade. She watched me overdose on pills before I flushed a different round of them. She watched me refuse diagnoses and interpret her concern as control. When she tried to participate in my care, she was refused: psychiatrists told her, politely, that they were not authorized to share information about my treatment; hospital administrators thanked her for her concern and turned her away. She went home and opened her journal.

When patients lack awareness of their illness, the people who love them carry a particular kind of weight—not only the practical burden, but the lonelier one of having to hold the truth for someone who cannot. What my mother experienced was an asymmetry so profound it constituted its own kind of grief: she could see what I could not see, and the system designed to protect me had no mechanism for honoring what she knew. What that costs, and what the law does and doesn't do with it, is the subject of a future column.

For now, the more fundamental thing: the instrument was broken, and I could not know it was broken, and the not-knowing was the condition.

Source: Nik Shuliahin/StockSnap

I first read the word anosognosia inside a state forensic psychiatric hospital, in Vince Granata's Everything Is Fine, a memoir about his brother's schizophrenia and the violence that came with it. Reading him in that place, at that hour, reordered everything. I had been carrying shame—the conviction that the cruelty had been me, expressed at last. Granata gave me a different frame. What I had done was real, and it had hurt the people I loved most. But the part of me that had done it had been operating with a faculty offline.

Shame is what you feel when you believe the self that acted is the only self there is. Guilt is what you feel when you know there is more to you than what the illness made you do—and when you grieve, on behalf of the people you hurt, that the more-than was not available.

Five more years of catastrophe followed the pill-flushing. Then lithium, then time, then the slow return of ground beneath my feet. The reading—Ghaemi, Amador, Lear, Granata—came once I had enough ground to sit with a book and recognize what had happened to me in it.

What I found was not the old self, restored intact. That self could not survive what came after, and didn't. What I found was something formed in the wake of the collapse: a self that had passed through the illness and could now look back on it with clarity, with sorrow, and with a kind of tenderness for the person who had been blind.

That is what anosognosia forecloses while it lasts: the witness who can see clearly what once could not be seen. To write about it from the other side, as I do now, is to perform the very act the condition once made impossible. Which means this essay is not only a description of the blindness. It is evidence that the blindness ends.

I did not choose it. I am choosing, now, to describe it—in the hope that someone still inside it, or loving someone who is, might find it worth holding.

item.title: What Ornette Coleman Teaches Us About the Creative Context
item.description:
Cognition

What Ornette Coleman Teaches Us About the Creative Context

Author Luke Burgis argues for the importance of liminal spaces.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Research finds that moviegoers will eat popcorn even if it's stale.
  • Luke Burgis' "The One and the Ninety-Nine" explores how context silently influences our creative behavior.
  • He points to Ornette Coleman, who built spaces that removed cues, freeing creators from audience pressures.
  • Liminal spaces break feedback loops, but work best as temporary resets rather than permanent states.
Research finds that we eat popcorn when we don't feel like it, but only in a familiar context
Source: Photo by Meg Boulden via Unsplash

As the lights go down in the movie theatre, you reflexively reach into the bucket of popcorn on your lap and start eating. You notice that the first bite is a bit stale, but you persist. By the time the previews are over, you look down and are shocked at what you see. How did you consume half the bucket without a thought?

The answer, in short, is the power of context.

A 2009 study at Duke University found that habitual moviegoers would eat popcorn in a theater regardless of whether they were full, and regardless of whether the popcorn was any good. Researchers intentionally made some of it stale. Didn't matter. In a movie theater, habitual popcorn eaters ate popcorn.

But when those same people were moved to a school library, the spell broke. They rejected the popcorn when they were full. They rejected it when it tasted bad. As the research paper distills, "People, when they perform a behavior a lot, outsource the control of the behavior to the environment."

The context cues the behavior, the behavior reinforces the context, and before long, we've handed over the keys without realizing we were ever holding them. This is true of snacking, and it's true of something considerably more consequential: how we create.

What Is Audience Capture and How Does Context Influence Creators?

Audience capture is the process by which creators gradually orient their work around the perceived preferences of their audience. It's driven by the social media feedback loop, and some of us are better than others at resisting the pull.

But audience capture is also a contextual phenomenon. Luke Burgis, in his new book The One and the Ninety-Nine, helps us zoom out on the bigger picture. Burgis, who writes extensively about mimetic desire and the social forces that shape what we want, explores environments that either reinforce or dissolve those forces. He draws on the anthropologist Victor Turner's concept of "anti-structures": social environments in which traditional roles, status hierarchies, and behavioral norms are temporarily suspended. They are, in effect, liminal contexts, devoid of traditional norms and expectations.

And the figure he returns to most vividly is the jazz musician Ornette Coleman. Coleman's story, as Burgis describes it, is ultimately less about the musician himself and more about the rooms he played in, the ones he avoided, and the ones he eventually built.

The Hidden Psychology of Coleman's Contexts

Coleman grew up in segregated Fort Worth, Texas, and started playing alto saxophone around age 14, with almost no formal training. What he had instead was a series of rooms.

Ornette Coleman was a jazz pioneer
Source: Photo by John Matychuk on Unsplash

The jazz clubs Coleman played as a teenager were unruly, liminal places that blurred the line between concert venue, gambling hall, and brothel. People came to leave their ordinary lives behind. As Burgis writes, quoting Coleman's biographer Maria Golia, the jazz club "deserves a place alongside temple, amphitheater, and cathedral, for not just conveying higher values but generating them, night after night, dissolving the boundaries separating individuals from a shared experience of the present moment."

These rooms lacked the ordinary cues. There were no fixed expectations about what the music should sound like. And it was in one of these rooms, during a solo on the 1927 standard "Stardust," that Coleman first played the melody "from the outside," following the notes the song inspired in him rather than the ones people expected to hear. He was fired immediately.

Over the next decade, Coleman endured poverty, violence, and obscurity for refusing to play what audiences wanted. As Burgis described in a recent conversation: "He was willing to endure poverty for almost a decade, and seemed to be very conscious of the price that he was paying to make the kind of music that he was making, economically and socially."

Most creators can't afford that price. The research on Grammy winners tells us as much: even being nominated but not winning pushes artists toward more conformist, genre-bound music. Proximity to recognition, without the recognition itself, makes the pull of the audience stronger. Is there a less punishing way to loosen the audience's grip?

The Psychology of Context Meets the Power of Liminal Spaces

From a psychological standpoint, Turner's anti-structures work because they reverse the logic of the popcorn study. Where the movie theater cues habitual behavior by providing familiar signals, the anti-structure liberates by removing them. You don't know what's expected of you, or of anyone else, and so the habitual pull weakens. There's genuine jeopardy in this unpredictability, but there's also a rare freedom. The environment provides no instructions.

A liminal space is a physical or psychological state of transition: The "in-between" zone
Source: Photo by Scarbor Siu via Unsplash

Coleman seemed to understand this intuitively. He eventually stopped just finding anti-structures and started building them. In 1968, he bought a loft in SoHo at 131 Prince Street and turned it into a space he called "Artists House," giving space to other musicians for almost nothing. There was no stage-audience divide, no traditional hierarchy, no familiar cues telling anyone what the music was supposed to sound like. As Burgis writes, "Coleman, at this stage in his life, was interested in creating places where new relationships could emerge outside of traditional contexts."

The loft jazz era it helped spawn was short-lived, but the creative output was extraordinary. The lesson from Coleman's lofts is that the spaces where audience capture loses its grip share specific features: the usual status markers are absent, the feedback loops are disrupted, and the people in the room don't yet know what to expect from each other or from themselves.

These liminal spaces can be physical or digital, formal or improvised. Burgis describes a friend who hosts cocktail hours with a single rule: nobody is allowed to say what they do for work. That's an anti-structure. So is seeking out people in their own in-between stages, and gathering in that shared uncertainty. One key insight from Turner, which Burgis emphasizes throughout the book, is that anti-structures aren't meant to last forever. As Burgis put it: "Most of us spend almost none of our time in anti-structures. I'm not advocating to just live in it, but to have the right amount."

The familiar context, trained on our past habits, has a vicelike grip on our behavior. You eat what you always eat, without thinking, without hardly tasting what you consume. In a liminal space, the unfamiliar context provides a greater, richer set of possibilities.

item.title: Why Trying to Love Yourself Can Make You Feel Worse
item.description:
Self-Help

Why Trying to Love Yourself Can Make You Feel Worse

Self-help advice can overlook how self-worth actually develops.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • We don't choose how we feel about ourselves. We learn it in relationships.
  • Positive thinking alone can't heal wounds that formed long before we understood words.
  • When self-help doesn't work, people often blame themselves or think that something is wrong with them.
  • Willpower does not heal relational wounds. Safe, stable, and consistent relationships do.
Source: Katrin Bolovtsova/Pexels

A video has been making the rounds on social media. In it, a well-known speaker warmly and confidently says, “How you feel about yourself is the most important choice you will ever make. These negative thoughts about yourself only persist because you keep choosing to believe them. If you repeat a different thought, you will become a different person.” I watched the clip and understood its intention, but I also felt a tightness in my chest.

I believe this message gets something fundamentally wrong.

We do not simply choose how we feel about ourselves. That process begins long before we can choose.

Our relationship with ourselves is shaped through thousands of developmental and relational experiences that become part of how we see ourselves and the world.

The problem is, I’ve worked with many people who tried exactly what was suggested. They chose, affirmed, journaled, and repeated these steps. They did everything they were told, but years later, they came to see me feeling even more ashamed than before. They were told the solution was simple, but when it didn’t work, they believed something must be wrong with them.

Life is complex. Our relationship to ourselves is complex. It is not all or nothing. It is everything, all at once.

How do we come to feel what we feel about ourselves?

Our relationship with ourselves doesn’t start in adulthood or with a thought we choose to believe. It begins in our earliest months, shaped by the kind of attention we receive, whether our needs are met or ignored, and whether being close to our caregivers feels safe or uncertain.

The brain develops from the bottom up. Early experiences with caregivers help shape the systems responsible for safety, stress regulation, and connection. When a child’s stress response is activated too often, development is disrupted, leaving later emotional and relational capacities built on a less stable foundation (Gertel Kraybill, 2018).

We don’t remember these early experiences as clear memories. Instead, they are stored in our bodies, shaping our automatic expectations and our sense of what it means to connect with others. These early patterns become the framework for how we see everything that comes after.

This isn’t simply important for people with a trauma diagnosis. It matters to all of us. Everyone experiences moments of misattunement. Even the most attentive caregiver cannot meet every need. According to Schore and Schore (2008), these breaks are a normal part of development. What matters is repair. When caregivers reconnect, children learn that relationships can survive disconnection and return to safety.

But if misattunement keeps happening and there’s no repair, a different lesson is learned. The nervous system starts to believe that relationships are unpredictable and unsafe. Needs feel risky, and being on guard seems safer than trusting. Underlying the struggles that follow is usually a strong effort to connect in whatever way the person knows how (Gertel Kraybill, 2018).

This pattern isn’t limited to severe neglect or abuse. Most of us fall somewhere along a spectrum of relational experiences. The intensity differs, but the underlying process is the same.

Children who do not frequently experience attunement are unable to form secure attachments. And this applies not only to relationships with others, but also to their relationship with themselves, to their own needs, their own sense of being worthy of care (Gertel Kraybill, 2018).

Where self-help culture misses the mark

The wellness industry doesn’t mean harm. Most people giving self-improvement advice genuinely want to help. But the message behind most of these suggestions, no matter how kindly they’re shared, is that you can change how you feel about yourself right now if you want it enough. So if you haven’t changed, it feels like you just didn’t want it badly enough.

For someone who already believes deep down that they aren’t enough, this isn’t encouragement. It feels like proof.

Oversimplifying this process can cause real harm. When people don’t get the promised results, they rarely blame the method. They blame themselves. I see this every week in people who have followed every piece of advice they could find, only to conclude that they are the problem.

What can help

I’m not saying change is impossible. I’ve seen significant change take place, and I’ve experienced it myself. But the way change really happens isn’t what most self-help advice describes. We don’t change just by picking better thoughts or deciding to love ourselves. Changing negative thoughts to positive ones isn’t enough.

Real change happens when we feel safe. More specifically, it’s about feeling safe in relationships. This sense of safety, predictability, and connection to ourselves develops through our relationships with others (Gertel Kraybill, 2018). If our nervous system learned to expect threat in relationships, it can only learn safety through new, safe relationships.

This isn’t only an idea. It’s how our nervous system actually works. The aim of trauma integration is to help people deeply feel that they are safe, worthy, and lovable. This isn’t a mental exercise. It develops slowly through relationships where those experiences are real.

One of the most powerful moments in therapy is when someone realizes: This isn’t who I am. It’s something that happened to me. And now I’m doing something about it (Gertel Kraybill, 2018). That understanding doesn’t come from thinking differently. It comes from experiencing a relationship that feels safe enough to support it.

It is not realistic, and that matters

It’s not realistic to think someone can simply decide to feel differently about themselves. Insight, willpower, or repetition alone can’t change nervous system patterns that were formed before we had language, memory, or the ability to choose.

It’s also unrealistic to expect this work to be quick. Developmental trauma needs a complex response and affects every part of our well-being: emotional, mental, physical, spiritual, and social (Gertel Kraybill, 2018). Even for people without a trauma diagnosis, changing how we feel about ourselves through relationships is slow, unpredictable, and deeply human.

When we pretend this work is easy and it isn’t, the people who get hurt most are those who are already vulnerable. They chase the promised results, don’t reach them, and add that disappointment to the burdens they already carry.

There are no shortcuts and no simple happy endings. Life and our relationship with ourselves are complex. It’s not all or nothing. It’s everything at once. This work invites patience, honesty, and the safety of a therapeutic relationship rather than chasing a version of healing that doesn’t reflect reality.

Healing is the slow, relational work of learning to live with what is, to its fullest. Not only joy, but grief. Not only confidence, but uncertainty. Not only the parts of ourselves we like, but all of who we are.

item.title: Eyewitness Testimony and Internal States
item.description:
Memory

Eyewitness Testimony and Internal States

Why recall failures can look like deception in forensic settings.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • State-dependent learning can explain why witnesses may forget details, not necessarily deceive.
  • Recognition tests, like multiple choice, reveal knowledge even when direct recall fails.
  • No objective test, including lie detectors, reliably identifies deception in courtrooms.

Is it possible for someone to know something but not know that they know it? If so, how would such a person be distinguished from someone who knows something but lies about it when asked? Interrogators and criminal investigators are faced with such conundrums all the time.

What is State-Dependent Learning?

In the 1960s researcher Donald Overton suggested that the likelihood of successful learning is greatest when there is a clear correlation between the circumstances which prevail while forming a memory, and during subsequent retrieval of that memory. Included here are both internal states, such as mood, alertness and attention, along with external conditions (temperature, nearby sounds or smells). Overton referred to this as “state-dependent learning”.

As an example, Overton tested rats learning to successfully wend their way through a maze while under the influence of pentobarbital. When later tested without the drug they failed to run the maze. Restoration of the pentobarbital led to a renewal of the rat’s successful performance.

Many of the findings on state dependent learning date from the 1960s, principally the work of Overton. His seminal 1964 paper “State-dependent or dissociated learning produced with pentobarbital” essentially defined the field. A person too may retain a memory, but the memory may be inaccessible, because conditions present when creating the memory were different during attempts at memory retrieval.

How State-Dependent Learning Affects Human Memory Retrieval

Thus memories are not stored like a video disc—an unalterable conveyor of established information—but as a relationship between the conditions that prevailed when the memory was encoded, compared to the conditions prevailing at the time of being asked about the memory. If the conditions differ sufficiently, the memory, if it exists, may be irretrievable.

As an example, people suffering from panic attacks often prove resistant to persuasion and even formal psychotherapy. That’s because the calmness of the discussion with the friend or therapist was totally different from the mentally tumultuous experience associated with the subsequent panic attack. In other words, both the external and internal cues present during the panic attack were totally opposite to the cues experienced during the previous help session.

A similar thing happens when a person is caught up in anger, stress or anxiety. When under the influence of these emotions, it’s hard to recall and put to use advice previously received from friends and therapists about remaining calm.

So the answer to our first question at the beginning of this essay is Yes. A failure of coming up with a memory (retrieval failure) doesn’t necessarily mean the interrogatee hasn’t retained some memory of it. But the only way of proving this is by testing for recognition memory, rather than retrieval memory. In other words, testing for whether they recognize the memory when they can’t retrieve it upon request. In students this takes the form of multiple-choice testing, whereby the student who cannot respond when asked for the correct answer nevertheless identifies it from a menu of possible choices only one of which is correct.

Wouldn’t it seem reasonable to assume that the student couldn’t recognize the correct answer if they hadn’t previously learned it? Inevitably in discussions about such situations, the issue of guessing arises. The student may even say “I was only guessing.” Although that claim can’t be disproven, an equally likely explanation holds that they did know the information (the test they had just taken demonstrated it!) but didn’t know that they knew it. An incorrect answer, in contrast, is a fairly reliable indicator that the information never was incorporated or encoded within the brain, and therefore cannot be retrieved because, simply, there is no memory to be retrieved.

State-Dependent Learning and Eyewitness Testimony

In the courtroom state-dependent learning provides an explanation for the unreliability of eye-witness testimony. Difficult emotional states may have characterized the events the eyewitness saw and is now recalling. But the internal and external cues may differ dramatically: witnessing, say, a violent assault versus later describing that crime while sitting in the comparatively calm atmosphere of the courtroom.

Typically, even the most cooperative of witnesses possesses more information than comes up during conventional questioning. The problem is not storage, but retrieval. The skillful interrogator is tasked with facilitating that retrieval without denigrating the witness.

The most important quality of a good interrogator is the ability to resist prematurely concluding the subject is lying, strictly on the basis of a “gut feeling” created by interview cues (the suspect appeared nervous, couldn’t maintain eye contact etc.). In the recent past interrogators have switched their emphasis from behavioral observations to the search for some physiological instrument for determining falsehood, starting with the lie detector test and extending to alterations in measurable brainwave forms elicited by physiological stimulation. None of these quasi objective tests have held up and, as a result, are not routinely used in courtroom determinations.

The Daubert Standard and Scientific Evidence for Detecting Lies

Phrased slightly differently, no method, technique, or instrument has passed the Daubert standard—established by the Supreme Court in 1993 in Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc. to address whether scientific evidence when presented by an expert should be accepted by a court.

Currently no claimed “objective” tests for lying have been accepted under Daubert as a reliable indicator that someone is lying. So the answer to the second question raised at the beginning of this essay is: Currently there is no objective test that infallibly identifies someone who knows something but lies about it. The standard for detecting concealed knowledge is slightly less stringent but, in general, the answer is still No when it comes to introducing such findings into a courtroom.

Ironically, the accuracy of the oldest method “the Lie Detector Test (LDT)” is only slightly better than chance, according to the social psychologist Aldert A. Vrij (“Outsmarting the Liars: Towards a Cognitive Lie Detection Approach”). Nonetheless, it has been applied within the past two years in the White House, the FBI and in several large organizations.

Nor is it probable that the idea that lying can somehow be reliably identified by some scientific test likely to be accepted in the courts any time soon. Why? Since lengthy prison terms or even capital punishment remain as a potential consequence of “proving” somebody a liar in court, the tolerated margin of error must be near zero. No currently available “brain test” comes even close to meeting that criteria.

Richard M. Restak, M.D.

item.title: Are You Living an Authentic Life?
item.description:
Authenticity

Are You Living an Authentic Life?

Ask yourself four questions to to discover how authentic you are.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Authenticity is about being open and honest with ourselves.
  • Being authentic is about becoming the self you could be.
  • Being true to ourselves is about unlearning who we think we should be.

Most of us have, at some time or another, been advised just to be ourselves. Perhaps it was before a job interview or a first date. Maybe it is advice we ourselves have given to others. It is probably the best advice a person can ever get. At the same time, it is also the worst.

The best because authenticity really is the key to a more fulfilling life. The research clearly shows that more authentic people are happier and more satisfied in their lives. But the worst because the phrase itself, “to be yourself,” is a flimsy expression that fails to convey the complexity of what it means to lead an authentic life. It is always going to be a problem trying to articulate a nuanced philosophical notion in a pithy sentence. It confuses as much as it enlightens.

But it is a phrase that is deeply entrenched in popular culture and has become a mantra in the self-help movement, encouraging people to express themselves openly and honestly rather than pretend to be someone they are not to please others.

But I will add another interpretation. The other people we might want to please are often not directly in front of us but can be voices in our minds that echo from the past. They might be the voices of teachers or parents from long ago in our lives. But they have become voices so deep within us that we don’t actually recognize them as coming from others. They are voices so familiar that they seem like our own.

Seen like this, the advice to be yourself might be better interpreted as not pretending to ourselves to be someone we are not, and learning to be open and honest with ourselves.

Authenticity means understanding ourselves, having awareness of our inner bodily, emotional, and cognitive states, being honest with ourselves, and possessing the ability to be openly expressive of these states with others. But it doesn’t mean that we always have to say whatever is on our mind; it is as much about knowing when to keep quiet.

Indeed, the idea that authenticity is always about saying what you think or feel is one of the most common misperceptions about the concept. Authenticity is, first and foremost, about what goes on inside a person.

Colloquially, we talk about being ourselves, but when we get deep into what authenticity is, it is more accurate to say that it is more about not being the self you are but becoming the self you could be.

Authenticity means going through the difficult process of unlearning the deep-seated conditions we have internalized about who we should be—a task that is ongoing over a lifetime.

Each day we make hundreds of small decisions. A lot of the time, we might do so without much thought. We are on automatic pilot, running on the voices in our minds that echo from the past. Authenticity is about being open and honest with ourselves about the decisions we make in each and every moment and how we make them.

Ask yourself the following questions:

  • Do you feel free to make your own choices?
  • Do you feel free to express your views and opinions?
  • Do you feel you can be yourself on a day-to-day basis?
  • Do you feel you are completely honest with yourself?

If you said no to any of these questions—and especially to the last question—you might be living a life that is less true to yourself than you would like. We can change our lives by striving for greater authenticity, but it is an ongoing, lifelong journey. It is a journey that starts right now, and in each and every small moment of our lives, and the choices we make, and how much our decisions and actions are the result of us being open and honest with ourselves.

Excerpted from my book Authentic: How to Be Yourself and Why It Matters.

item.title: Power Play: Romance and Hockey Culture
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

Power Play: Romance and Hockey Culture

Personal Perspective: Romance novels are transforming hockey culture. The world is here for it.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Hockey romances effectively address problems with hockey culture.
  • Hockey romances written by women bring a unique lens to the dynamics of hockey culture.
  • Hockey organizations should partner with romance series creators to make long-overdue changes.

Romance and rape surround hockey’s embattled identity like overlapping figure eights, but a new record-breaking hockey romance series offers valuable insights for how to repair this complex sport many of us struggle to love.

Inspired by Elle Kennedy’s best-selling book series of the same name, a central plot in the 8-episode streaming sensation Off Campus is the rape of lead character Hannah Wells by a man whose high-profile status as a hockey player and son of the town mayor leads to a slanderous court trial against Wells. Hailed by survivors for its validating treatment of sexual assault, the series follows Hannah as she processes flashbacks, navigates disclosure, and reclaims her sexuality in a relationship with the star hockey player on the fictional Briar University team.

Weeks after the show aired, North Carolina Hurricane fans shouted the anti-sexual violence slogan “no means no” at Las Vegas Golden Knights goaltender Carter Hart during the Stanley Cup Finals. One of the five players on Canada’s 2018 World Juniors hockey team who were acquitted on charges of sexual assault on July 24, 2025, Hart has had a stellar year with the Knights. The fans' chanting, though, reflects widespread fatigue with the injustice that plagues hockey culture when it comes to sexual assault by its players and the organizations that thrive on secrets over transparency. Videos of the chant went viral and there have been thousands of online responses like: “Finally! Been waiting for this chant since he re-entered the league!” and “so tired of men getting away with these horrendous crimes against women.”

This anger coincides with a massive global appetite for alternate depictions of sexual violence and masculinity in hockey culture. We saw this with Heated Rivalry, and hockey series written by Becka Mack, Helena Hunting, and Lexi Lafleur Brown—all Canadian—are also serial bestsellers. Romance invites readers into the world of hockey, but their love of the game and what it could be keeps them turning the pages and watching the series, often repeatedly.

The world is watching what happens in hockey in more ways than one.

If hockey associations want to change their image and the lives of the players inside its cloistered walls they should pay attention to what this powerful new series has to offer. NHL commissioner Gary Bettman claims to have binge-watched both Off Campus and Heated Rivalry, so why not leverage what this romance does well to help Canadians fall back in love with our national sport?

Hockey Canada and allied groups could partner with the producers and cast of Off Campus to co-create media content about the white elephant in the room that the series gets right: sexual assault. Men must see other men questioning hockey’s tradition of sexual assault and violence more broadly (i.e., fighting, hazing) to shift the cultural needle. Showing men sharing their knowledge about consent in sexual relationships and expressing fears around vulnerable forms of intimacy could also impact the culture in a big way.

As suggested by shelters and anti-violence groups across the country, hockey organizations should be pouring resources into public conferences, media partnerships, and educational efforts to change the legislative approach to sexual assault in Canada. Updating the public about these events and developments is also key.

That sexual assault survivors in Canada may feel more validated by a streaming series than by a courtroom is a travesty that exposes failures across hockey and the legal system, and persistent sexism. In a world where hockey players are still too often treated like gods who skate far above the ranks of the people whose lives they impact, romance is proving time and again to be one of the most powerful and accessible ways to transform the violence that plagues hockey culture.

item.title: False Prophets? Mental Health Misinformation Online
item.description:
Social Media

False Prophets? Mental Health Misinformation Online

What research tells us about how we're misled by medical info online.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Social media is a prominent source of mental health misinformation.
  • Trauma, ADHD, ASD, suicide, personality disorders, and psychosis are common subjects of misinformation.
  • Exposure to misinformation and health literacy are two key variables in the vulnerability to being misled.
  • Barriers to safety and trust with professionals raise issues at a higher level within the healthcare system.
Source: Alexandra_Koch/Pixabay

Misinformation about mental health has been identified across various online spaces, including Facebook, Reddit, and, prominently, TikTok. In 2021, the U.S. Surgeon General even named health misinformation as a public health crisis, and for good reason. Mental health misinformation can:

  • Increase stigma and perpetuate prejudice, discrimination, and rejection from others
  • Pathologize normal experiences
  • Misattribute symptoms of one disorder to another (i.e., some diagnoses are more “popular” than others on social media)

All of which ultimately thwarts self-understanding, intensifies widespread problems of isolation and loneliness, and interferes with getting the appropriate treatment.

The frightening truth is that the public is regularly exposed to, believes, and acts on information that is inaccurate, misleading, and/or outright harmful. However, the average person still faces real barriers to accessing accurate information from trustworthy sources. So, as you and others in your life voyage out into the murky waters of online self-education, consider what recent research has revealed about online mental health misinformation, what increases the risk of being misled, and how we can protect ourselves against misleading or outright false pieces of information.

What’s Out There

Starvaggi and colleagues (2024) reviewed, summarized, and offered reflections on the state of mental health misinformation on social media. The article presents an overall concerning picture of mental health misinformation on TikTok (i.e., 31 percent deemed “scientifically inaccurate” and 14 percent “potentially damaging”). Nonetheless, it seems that certain topics are more subject to misinformation than others.

One study found misinformation to be particularly common around the subjects of suicide, personality disorders, psychosis, and treatment (Hudon et al., 2025), whereas another report found that trauma-related and neurodevelopmental disorders (e.g., ADHD and ASD) featured the highest rates of misinformation. By the numbers, this broke down to only 33 percent of trauma-related content being considered “scientifically accurate.” For neurodevelopmental disorders, the misinformation problems are varied.

For example, videos about ADHD (Yeung et al., 2022):

  • More scientifically accurate, but highest rate of “potentially damaging” content (18 percent)
  • Still, 52 percent of videos had “information lacking scientific evidence” (e.g., signs and symptoms of ADHD)

Videos about ASD (Aragon et al., 2023):

  • Of the videos reviewed, 27 percent were accurate, 41 percent were inaccurate, and 32 percent were potentially misleading (e.g., overgeneralizing characteristics of individuals with ASD)

Vulnerability to Misinformation

Recent studies have found that greater exposure to misinformation and lower health literacy are two prominent risk factors for agreeing with mental health misinformation in online communities (Bizzotto et al., 2023; Hoffner et al., 2026). In other words, the more content that is out there and the more we see it (exposure), the more vulnerable we are to believing information that is inaccurate, misleading, and/or dangerous. Moreover, the less we know about mental health from reliable, accurate sources (health literacy), the greater our chances of being led astray.

Interestingly, self-efficacy appears to be another key variable in how people engage with misinformation online in that those with higher self-efficacy indicated greater intentions to respond to, rather than ignore, posts with misinformation. Meaning, people who believe they can have an active influence on others and the world around them act in ways that suggest a level of self-worth and empowerment to help protect others by preserving factual integrity.

In Safety We Trust (and Learn)

So long as there are real barriers to accessing quality mental health services and information, people in need will naturally, and resourcefully, find alternative means of care and education. The noticeable rise in young people turning to TikTok for mental health information during the COVID-19 pandemic reflected this quite well (Lee, 2022).

Furthermore, the issues of mistrust in the mental healthcare system are well-documented both off- and online. Individual and communal experiences of invalidation, underdiagnosis, and generally low-quality care reasonably motivate hurt, scared, and frustrated individuals to seek and find the validation they desire from peers in online communities. The real and important sense of safety and belongingness is one proposed link between exposure to and agreement with mental health misinformation. In contrast to the safety and trust derived in these communities, one study found that only half of the 37 percent of participants who were influenced by advice they encountered in online communities consulted a professional about the changes they were making in the management of their illness (Tan et al., 2021).

Although rampant online, health misinformation isn’t new, and it isn’t going anywhere. While regulations and fact-checking mechanisms are useful safeguards, they do not address some of the most important underlying drivers for how misinformation gains traction in our minds and mental health decisions. When professionals do not satisfactorily respond to needs for empathy, validation, and trust, those professionals will, at best, sound like an adult in the Charlie Brown universe to a person seeking not only information, but also care and compassion.

Therefore, it is incumbent upon providers to address issues of trust in their interactions with patients and the public. However, as Jon Allen (2022) goes through great lengths to unpack, conceptualize, and offer some guidance on in his book, Trusting in Psychotherapy, becoming trustworthy as a mental health professional remains a major gap in formal training and education.

Yet, blaming individuals or even groups of professionals also likely misses the bigger picture. Healthcare professionals across settings are facing growing pressure to conform their approach to treatment according to the priorities of insurance companies and private equity groups, which privilege easily quantifiable, replicable, and financially conservative modes of treatment (Cotton, 2025; Michaels, 2025). In and of itself, this may not sound like a problem, but when these treatment models insidiously (and inaccurately) determine that the time and training required to genuinely establish trust with people who both need and fear mental health treatment the most is inefficient and too complex to quantify, then it is no wonder that people turn to the approachable voices online.
